Symmetry constraints associated with the cluster partition and excitation reduce the coupled system, while the corresponding group transformations recover the complete response in the retained coordinates. To assess overall efficiency, we evaluate the costs of local construction, propagation, global solution, and recovery. Numerical examples involving layered and finite annular patch arrays show close agreement between the computed and reference complex far fields and shorter complete-run times than those of the corresponding symmetry-reduced direct solvers. Among the three equivalent-source implementations for the layered array, the one with the smallest coupled system has the longest runtime because local construction and propagation dominate the cost. These findings highlight the need to consider local construction and coupling costs when assessing the benefit of reducing the global system dimension.

items.title: A Telescopic Method with Guaranteed B-Stationarity for Partitioned Cardinality and Complementarity Constraints
items.summary: We consider the minimization of a smooth function subject to box constraints and partitioned cardinality constraints (PCC): the variables are divided into groups and, within each group, at most a prescribed number of variables may be non-zero. This class contains bound-constrained minimization, cardinality-constrained minimization and bound-constrained mathematical programs with complementarity constraints. We introduce the Telescopic Method, which alternates iterations of a bound-constrained method on the faces of the feasible set with inexpensive one-dimensional "escaping" tests that exchange a variable of the current face by a currently null one within the same group. We prove, without constraint qualifications and without requiring global solutions of subproblems, that every limit point of the generated sequence is B-stationary, i.e., it satisfies the first-order condition defined by the tangent cone of the feasible set. This guarantee is obtained with exchanges of a single variable, whatever the number of non-null entries of the limit point, because B-stationarity for this class of problems decomposes into conditions on single variables. On the 60 bound-constrained mathematical programs with complementarity constraints of the test set of Kirches, Larson, Leyffer and Manns, the method found approximately B-stationary points in all the problems. Applications to separable regression, sparse polynomial approximation and portfolio selection are described and tested numerically.

items.title: The covering radius of the first-order Reed-Muller code in nine variables is 242
items.summary: We prove that the covering radius of the binary first-order Reed-Muller code RM(1,9) is exactly 242. Equivalently, the maximum nonlinearity of a Boolean function in nine variables is 242. Our proof combines a one-point rigidity theorem with a spectral and computational exclusion of the two larger candidate nonlinearities. We first show that every nine-variable Boolean function of nonlinearity 243 admits a unique one-point modification that raises its nonlinearity to 244: the point to be changed is the vector sum of its support. This part uses exact Walsh-update identities, integer interpolation, rigidity of a quadratic residue, and a sharp Walsh l1 estimate for cubic Boolean functions. To exclude nonlinearity 244, we use Parseval's identity and congruences of integral Walsh coefficients to force an exceptionally restricted spectrum. An associated cubic residue phase must attain the extremal Walsh l1 bound 10240. We eliminate one equality spectrum by hyperplane slicing; the other forces the original Boolean function from the signs of the cubic phase and yields a double-complement-pairing identity for its cubic top part. The classification of alternating trilinear forms over F2, an exact filter of their representatives, and two exhaustive enumerations of 218 quadratic supplements then rule out every remaining candidate. Together with the known construction attaining nonlinearity 242, these arguments establish the asserted covering radius.

items.title: Differential Privacy for Generalized Entropy Indices of Income Inequality
items.summary: The mean log deviation and the Theil index are two widely used measures of income inequality. The organization releasing these measures may be obligated to protect the confidentiality of the individual incomes used in the computations. In particular, the organization may wish to release versions of these measures with formal guarantees of privacy. The organization could do so by satisfying differential privacy; however, typical applications of differentially private algorithms are likely to add so much noise to the measures that they become unusable. We present differentially private algorithms for these indices with reasonable error properties. The algorithms rely on computing or approximating bounds on the smooth sensitivity, that is, the maximum absolute amount the inequality measures change when replacing any subset of the $n$ incomes in the reported data with arbitrarily chosen feasible values. For the mean log deviation, the algorithm runs in $O(n^2)$ time. For the Theil index, the algorithm runs in $O(n\log n)$ time. We illustrate the performance of each differentially private algorithm using individual-level and household-level income data from the Current Population Survey. We also examine repeated sampling properties of the algorithms using artificially generated data. The empirical results indicate when these differentially private algorithms can be expected to provide accurate estimates and when they are likely to introduce too much noise.

items.title: Service-Area Robust NOMA for Pinching Antennas Systems
items.summary: Pinching-antenna systems (PASS) enable near-field beam focusing using radiating points along a dielectric waveguide, but coherent spherical-wave superposition makes their channels sensitive to small user displacements. This sensitivity is critical for power-domain non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA), where successive interference cancellation (SIC) requires the weak-user layer to remain decodable at the strong user. We develop spatially robust PASS-NOMA designs that optimize antenna placement and power splitting over bounded service areas (SAs), with a preset decoding order and explicit SIC-feasibility constraints. We propose a worst-case design for quasi-static users and an ergodic design for codewords spanning representative SA positions, and characterize their achievable rate regions. Numerical results show that, despite SIC requiring weak-user decoding in both SAs, NOMA outperforms orthogonal multiple access (OMA) with a shared placement under both robustness models except when the strong user is served at low rate. In the ergodic regime, this advantage can persist even against OMA with per-user antenna reconfiguration.

items.title: A structure-preserving finite volume scheme for the time-fractional Allen-Cahn equation with nondegenerate state-dependent mobility
items.summary: We construct and analyze a fully discrete finite volume scheme for the time-fractional Allen-Cahn equation with nondegenerate state-dependent mobility. The scheme combines a standard two-point flux approximation of diffusion, the L1 approximation of the Caputo derivative on a uniform time grid, and a semiconvex splitting of the potential, and it discretizes the inverse mobility by a secant average multiplying the entire L1 derivative. The key estimate is a lower bound for the accumulated pairing of this weighted L1 derivative with the solution increments in terms of the accumulated L1 quadratic form. Using this lower bound, we derive a discrete energy estimate and the time regularity required for compactness. For twice continuously differentiable semiconvex potentials satisfying sign conditions outside $(-1,1)$ and initial data in $H^1(Ω)$ taking values in $[-1,1]$, we prove existence of at least one fully discrete solution on every admissible finite volume mesh and every uniform time grid. Every such solution satisfies the maximum bound principle and a discrete energy bound relative to the initial energy, without a time-step restriction. In up to three space dimensions, under a mesh regularity condition with a constant independent of the mesh size, we prove that any sequence of fully discrete solutions has a subsequence converging strongly in $L^2(Ω\times(0,T))$ to a weak solution of the continuous problem as the mesh size and time step tend to zero. As a consequence, we obtain existence of a weak solution in one and two space dimensions, and in three dimensions whenever such meshes exist.

items.title: Efficient second-order physics-preserving schemes for incompressible flows with variable density and viscosity
items.summary: This paper proposes a novel second-order prediction--filter--projection framework for incompressible flows with variable density and viscosity. In this framework, a constrained $L^2$-projection is enforced to unconditionally preserve the prescribed density bounds and discrete mass conservation, while a generalized-Laplacian reformulation combined with the D-CSAV approach is used to discretize the variable-viscosity momentum equation. In particular, a density-weighted second-order time filter is proposed, which eliminates the additional uniform-in-time bound restriction imposed on the time difference quotient of the discrete density in existing stability analyses. The resulting scheme is shown to satisfy an unconditional modified-energy dissipation law, without the viscosity-related restrictions imposed in earlier work. Then, an additional scalar auxiliary variable and its compatible temporal discretization are introduced to construct a variable-step prediction--filter--projection scheme. This scheme is also bound-preserving and mass-conserving, and satisfies an unconditional modified-energy dissipation law. Moreover, the modified energy is much closer to the ``original'' kinetic energy, differing from it only through the auxiliary-variable corrections. Based on the variable-step scheme, a reliable energy-based adaptive time-stepping strategy is developed. Finally, numerical experiments demonstrate the accuracy, physics-preserving properties, and efficiency of the proposed schemes.

items.title: When are dividend barriers optimal? A distributional characterization in renewal risk models
items.summary: We study the finite-horizon optimal dividend problem in a renewal risk model with unrestricted dividend payments, examining how claim-size distributions determine barrier optimality. Under general assumptions on a fixed interclaim-time distribution, we prove that exponential claims admit a globally optimal barrier for every positive safety loading, positive discount rate and finite horizon. Conversely, within the class of claim-size distributions with continuous nondecreasing hazard, every nonexponential law admits one fixed premium--discount pair for which no barrier is globally optimal at any sufficiently long horizon. These results establish, within this distribution class, an equivalence between exponentially distributed claims and the existence of a globally optimal barrier for every parameter combination in the stated range. Numerical examples compare exponential and Gamma claims with the same mean and illustrate how the claim-size distribution changes the structure of dividend decisions.

items.title: $\ell_{\infty}$ norm SVP in $\widetilde{O}(3^n)$
items.summary: We give a classical randomized algorithm for the Shortest Vector Problem in the infinity norm in $\widetilde O(3^n)$ time and space, improving the previous bound of $2^{2.443n+o(n)}$. We adapt Gaussian difference dynamics to the infinity norm by repeatedly taking differences of vectors from two lists, producing lists in successively smaller cubes. The key is to restrict the midpoint of each pair to a fixed inner cube, so that every allowed difference has the same region of possible midpoints. Using random lattice translates, this rule preserves equal expected counts at each point of the smaller cube. We analyze the dependencies created by repeated differencing through the counting moments of Gaussian difference dynamics, together with a weighted packing bound for cubes. Finally, two searches based on coordinate comparisons generate the intermediate lists and recover a shortest lattice vector within the claimed time bound.

items.title: Agent4FreeFem: A Verification-Guided Framework for Autonomous Topology Optimization
items.summary: Topology optimization has become an indispensable design tool in the aerospace, automotive, and mechanical engineering industries. Yet bringing a new problem from its description to an optimized result remains slow, expert-dependent, and unreliable: the workflow spans many manually connected stages, each new problem requires solver code to be written and debugged manually, and such code often fails or yields incorrect results. We present Agent4FreeFem, a pipeline driven by a large language model that turns a natural-language problem description into a set of verified optimization results without manual solver-code development or debugging. The pipeline keeps the problem definition unmodified, localizes errors using independent sources of evidence, and completes constrained repairs automatically, thereby providing efficient end-to-end automation, autonomous execution, and verifiable results. We evaluated Agent4FreeFem on a suite of single-physics and coupled multiphysics problems. Every case passed runtime verification and finished within the repair budget of each stage.

items.title: A Second-Order Stochastic Dynamic Mode Decomposition by Richardson Extrapolation
items.summary: Stochastic dynamic mode decomposition (SDMD) approximates the Koopman semigroup of an Itô diffusion by a Galerkin generator matrix on a dictionary of observables, computed from samples of the invariant law and evaluations of the generator, and advances observables with a first-order stochastic Taylor step (SDMD-1). The second-order Taylor step (SDMD-2) also needs the matrix of second generator actions, hence a dictionary with four derivatives, evaluations of a fourth-order differential operator at every sample, and a third matrix. We show that the Richardson extrapolation of two SDMD-1 half steps (SDMD-R) is second-order accurate with the data, the matrices, and the regularity of SDMD-1. One error bound covers exact and empirical Galerkin matrices. It consists of the Galerkin error of the dictionary, which is common to all schemes, a time-stepping term, and a data term of order $m^{-1/2}$ in the sample size $m$. The time-stepping term is $O(\dt^2)$ for SDMD-R and $O(Θ_N\dt+\dt^2)$ for SDMD-2, where $Θ_N$ is the norm of the second-order Galerkin residual $\Proj_N\cA(I-\Proj_N)\cA|_{\cV_N}$. The first-order term is attained and, for self-adjoint generators, vanishes only for generator-invariant dictionaries. For reversible periodic diffusions and trigonometric dictionaries with cutoff $K$, the step restriction $\dt\lesssim K^{-2}$ makes all three schemes contractions, and the error against the Koopman semigroup on $H^\ell$ observables is $O(K^{-(\ell-2)}+\dt^p)$ plus a sampling term of order $K^{d+2}m^{-1/2}$ in dimension $d$, with $p=1$ for SDMD-1 and $p=2$ for SDMD-R and SDMD-2. Numerical experiments confirm that SDMD-R matches or improves on the accuracy of SDMD-2 at the cost of SDMD-1.

items.title: Unbiased Low-Rank Approximation for Repeated Matrix-Vector Multiplication: Stability and Optimal Sampling
items.summary: Replacing the matrix in an iteration with random low-rank matrices can reduce the cost of matrix-vector multiplication. However, even if the sampled matrices equal the original matrix in expectation, the expected squared norm of the random iterates may grow while the original iteration converges. Under a fixed rank bound, we study how to choose the distribution of these random matrices to minimize this growth when sampling independently at each step. We derive an exact formula for the optimal asymptotic growth factor and use it to determine when the expected squared norm can converge to zero. We then characterize precisely when a fixed sampling distribution achieves this optimal factor and construct finite-support optimal distributions in every attainable case. These results determine the minimum rank required for stability and provide optimal sampling designs under the prescribed rank constraint.

items.title: Flux vector splittings and semi-implicit finite volume schemes for an isentropic two-phase flow model
items.summary: We present two new semi-implicit finite volume schemes for the 1D hyperbolic and thermodynamically compatible (HTC) isentropic two-phase flow model of Romenski et al., written in terms of mixture density, volume fraction, partial gas density, mixture momentum and the relative phase velocity. In gas-liquid mixtures, the sound speed of the weakly compressible liquid is much larger than the gas sound speed and flow velocity, so the time step of fully explicit discretizations is dictated by liquid acoustic waves, even when the interest lies in the dynamics of the gas. To overcome this difficulty, the model's flux is split at the continuous level into an explicit subsystem (gas dynamics) and an implicit subsystem (liquid acoustic waves), leading to a nonlinear system for liquid pressure solved with the Newton method. In the first splitting the entire liquid phase is treated implicitly, while in the second the liquid convective terms are moved to the explicit subsystem, so only liquid acoustic waves are treated implicitly and nested Picard iterations are avoided. Thus, the time step of both schemes is restricted only by flow velocities and gas sound speed, independent of liquid sound speed. We prove and numerically confirm that both schemes exactly preserve the Abgrall condition (uniform velocity and pressure across material interfaces). For well-prepared initial data, both schemes are consistent with the volume balance of the liquid's low Mach number limit. Riemann problems, pressure equilibrium tests and acoustic tests show that in non-stiff regimes the semi-implicit schemes reproduce the results of a fully explicit scheme, while in the stiff regime they allow time steps that are up to 3-4 orders of magnitude larger, avoiding the excessive numerical dissipation of explicit schemes whose numerical viscosity is dictated by liquid sound speed.

items.title: A posteriori error estimates for a finite volume approximation of a local sensing Keller-Segel model
items.summary: A local sensing Keller-Segel model, in which cells adjust their motility to the local chemoattractant rather than its gradient, and a semi-implicit finite volume scheme for its numerical approximation are studied. Computable a posteriori bounds for the approximation error measured in terms of the $L^\infty(0, T; H^{-1}(Ω))$ and $L^2(0, T; L^2(Ω))$ norms of the cell density are derived based on a new stability estimate and suitable reconstructions of the flux and the flux potential of the numerical solution. Optimal scaling of the estimates is numerically demonstrated in 1D and 2D experiments. Moreover, an adaptive mesh refinement method steered by the estimator is proposed for the 1D case, and its efficiency is numerically verified.

items.title: Edge-structure fault diameters of exchanged hypercubes
items.summary: We determine the edge-structure and edge-substructure fault diameters of the exchanged hypercube $EH(s,t)$ for every $1\le s\le t$. Both parameters equal $s+t+4$, two more than the fault-free diameter, except for $EH(2,2)$, where both are nine, and $EH(1,1)$, where they are five and six, respectively. This holds even though an admissible family may remove up to $2s$ vertices, more than the vertex connectivity $s+1$. For every $s\ge2$, the maximum is attained by $s$ parallel fault edges in class $0$. For $s\ge3$, the structure-fault diameter exceeds the classical $s$-vertex-fault diameter by exactly one.

items.title: Leaving Quantum Bias on the Table: Pushforwards as a Path to Quantum Advantage in Constrained Optimization
items.summary: Constrained quantum samplers often produce infeasible outputs that retain information about good feasible solutions. We develop a post-measurement framework that constructs problem-dependent classical feasibility maps from constraint-violation statistics and pushes the raw quantum sampling law forward onto the feasible set. The probability of each repaired solution is the total raw mass of its repair preimage, enlarging the successful sampling event from a target feasible set to its full repair preimage. We derive exact identities for repaired success and expected cost, and separate repair-basin geometry from sampler-dependent probability concentration. For noisy implementations, we distinguish leakage from the encoded subspace from concentration loss within it. For permutation constraints, Hungarian maximum-overlap repair provides an O(n^3) implementation, which we study on traveling-salesman problems (TSP). We derive conditional repaired-success bounds and quantify how basin aggregation reduces the absolute-transfer budget required by these bounds. Noiseless simulations show that optimal repair basins contain selectively overweighted infeasible contributors. For an n=10 TSP instance, pushforward repair recovered the optimum using approximately 10^3 shots, compared with 10^6 shots in the original CE-QAOA workflow without repair. On a 127-qubit IBM processor, using encodings of up to 100 qubits, repaired candidates match reference tours on smaller benchmarks and improve them on larger instances. These results establish concentration of quantum probability on useful repair preimages as a design principle for constrained quantum optimization.

items.title: Forgetting matters: when subspace optimization accelerates without the strong convexity parameter
items.summary: Sequential subspace optimization (SESOP) minimizes the objective exactly over a few directions built from past iterates. It needs no problem constants, is accelerated on smooth convex functions and behaves like an accelerated method in experiments. This led to the conjecture that it is accelerated in the strongly convex case without knowing the strong convexity parameter. We show that the conjecture fails in the worst case. For every subspace method whose memory forgets slowly, namely a window of recent gradients and steps together with cumulative sums with subexponential weights, we construct a counterexample: acceleration requires a window of length of order $\sqrtκ$, where $κ$ is the condition number. SESOP and the plane form of conjugate gradients are therefore not accelerated. Memories that forget fast avoid this obstruction. Pairs of geometric filters give accelerated methods with logarithmic memory or only two stored vectors. They need neither the strong convexity parameter nor the smoothness constant, never restart the iterate and restart their memory at most $O(\logκ)$ times. Finally, the method with fixed activation times remains asymptotically accelerated on functions with Lipschitz Hessian even when each subproblem is solved by a single Newton step.

items.title: Representation-Aware Closed-Surface Parameterization: Exact Sensitivity Analysis and Pole-Aware Planar Preconditioning
items.summary: Surface parameterization is a fundamental task in geometry processing and shape analysis. For topologically closed surfaces, it is common to parameterize them onto a standardized closed domain in $\mathbb{R}^3$, with a prime example being a unit sphere for genus-0 closed surfaces. Many mapping methods use planar projections and perform computations on the plane rather than directly on the 3D surface. However, perturbations introduced before projection or geometric evolution propagate through the computation and may affect map quality, convergence, stopping behavior, and geometric validity. In this work, we formulate representation sensitivity as a branchwise input--output problem, separating smooth propagation through active Jacobians from changes in anchors, stopping rules, and fallback events. Under consistent piecewise-linear assembly, the unmodified south-pole Beltrami correction in the FLASH method for spherical conformal parameterization reduces exactly to source-mesh harmonic extension. On a fixed-anchor branch, the corrected map factors into chart transition, harmonic propagation, and inverse stereographic projection, yielding an explicit sensitivity Jacobian and a finite-triangle conditioning bound. Separately, we introduce a bounded five-parameter affine preconditioner over planar scale, translation, and anisotropy and evaluate candidates on the corrected spherical map. Across 30 genus-0 surfaces, it reduces median polar upper-tail log-condition and chord-angle distortion by $10.17\%$ and $10.97\%$, respectively, with both measures improving on every mesh. We also apply the framework to other spherical mapping methods including the conformalized mean-curvature flow and spherical density-equalizing maps. Altogether, our work highlights the importance of representation selection as a structural and practical component of spherical parameterization and downstream computation.

items.title: ALDER: A Single-Loop Augmented-Lagrangian Damped Extragradient Method for Nonconvex--Concave Minimax Problems with Nonlinear Coupled Constraints
items.summary: ALDER, a single-loop augmented-Lagrangian damped extragradient method, is proposed for smooth nonconvex--concave minimax problems with nonlinear coupled inequality constraints. Within an augmented-Lagrangian framework, ALDER combines prediction--correction steps for the primal variables with explicit projected-and-relaxed multiplier updates in a single loop. The penalty parameter is fixed throughout each run, eliminating inner-loop subproblem solves and iterative penalty updates. We establish uniform boundedness of the relaxed multiplier sequence and, under an extended Mangasarian--Fromovitz constraint qualification, boundedness of the projected output multiplier. Building on these bounds, we show that ALDER finds an $\varepsilon$-KKT point within $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-7/2})$ complete first-order oracle evaluations in the strongly concave setting and $\mathcal{O}(\varepsilon^{-4})$ in the concave setting. These bounds improve upon the best known complexity bounds for multi-loop algorithms for this problem class, achieved by FAL, by removing a $\log(1/\varepsilon)$ factor, while retaining a single-loop update structure.

items.title: Testing MAX-CUT in the Adjacency Matrix Model: Tight Non-Adaptive Bounds and a Cubic Adaptive Lower Bound
items.summary: We study the query complexity of approximating the MAX-CUT value to additive error $\varepsilon n^2$ in the adjacency matrix model. This was one of the first problems studied in the area of graph property testing [GGR, JACM'1998]. Previously, the best known upper bound for both adaptive and non-adaptive algorithms was $O(1/\varepsilon^6)$ [MS, SODA'2008; GMRS, ICALP'2022]. The only known lower bound was a trivial $Ω(1/\varepsilon^2)$ bound. We close this gap from both sides for non-adaptive algorithms, proving that its query complexity is exactly $Θ(1/\varepsilon^4)$. We also prove an adaptive $Ω(1/\varepsilon^3)$ lower bound. Our upper bound is achieved by a canonical tester that samples $O(1/\varepsilon^2)$ vertices in expectation and outputs the rescaled MAX-CUT value of the induced subgraph. We prove its correctness by applying spectral truncation to the adjacency matrix, using a geometric argument to control the sampling error of the retained low-rank part and a cut-norm restriction estimate [RV, JACM'2007] for the remainder. As an application, an analogous proof also yields a tight $O(1/\varepsilon^4)$ non-adaptive query upper bound for MAX-2CSP. For our lower bounds, we show indistinguishability between a uniform random graph and a distribution that plants a hidden partition. For the non-adaptive lower bound, we observe that one plus the $χ^2$-divergence between the query transcript distributions is exactly a normalized Ising partition function, which can be bounded using Boolean hypercontractivity. For the adaptive lower bound, we view each query through the algorithm's ability to predict whether its endpoints lie in the same part of the hidden partition. We bound the combined advantage of these predictions using the completed transcript, which lets us analyze the adaptively chosen pairs together despite their dependence on earlier answers.

items.title: Parameter Bounds and Inverse Approximation for Linearized ReLU$^k$ Networks on the Sphere
items.summary: We study direct and inverse approximation for linearized shallow ReLU$^k$ networks on $\mathbb S^d$ with quasi-uniform hidden parameters. For $0<α<\frac{d+2k+1}{2d}$, under the coefficient growth condition $\bigl(n\sum_{j=1}^na_{j,n}^2\bigr)^{\frac{1}{2}}\leq n^αM$, we prove that approximation at the order $n^{-\frac{d+2k+1}{2d}+α}$ is equivalent to membership in the parity-compatible Besov space $\mathcal B_{2,\infty,*}^{\frac{d+2k+1}{2}-αd}(\mathbb S^d)$. Mere convergence under the same coefficient budget does not imply this regularity. For unconstrained approximation along a nested parameter sequence, a single ridge function gives a counterexample when $α<\frac{1}{2}$, whereas for $α>\frac{1}{2}$ the endpoint Besov inverse conclusion follows from a Bernstein inequality under antipodal quasi-uniformity. The inverse conclusion is also recovered when the prescribed rate holds for two quasi-uniform parameter sequences whose union is antipodally separated.

items.title: Equal Hamming Weights at Fixed Root Order and Applications to Constacyclic MDS Codes
items.summary: For a fixed positive integer $n>1$, we study the prime powers $q$ coprime to $n$ for which all monic irreducible factors of $Φ_n$ over $\F_q$ have the same coefficient Hamming weight. Cyclotomic orbit coefficients give a finite, effective classification of these fields. Outside finitely many computable characteristics, every factor has the support of its characteristic-zero orbit polynomial; the uniform condition $p>2^{\varphi(n)}$ suffices. In each remaining characteristic, extension exponents reduce to divisors of $\ord_n(p)$, and an integer variance identity expressed by polynomial gcd degrees decides equal weight. The same coefficient data determine the full weight distribution. As an application, we prove that an MDS constacyclic code with an irreducible generator forces every irreducible polynomial of the same root order to have full support, including factors associated with different constacyclic constants. This yields a uniform gcd and norm obstruction. We develop its short-multiplier extension, give a prime-order cubic family, and establish an explicit quadratic-residue exclusion without a prime-square alphabet or a near-square length hypothesis.

items.title: Log-Driven Semantic Tuning for Mixed Integer Programming Solvers
items.summary: Automated configuration of mixed-integer programming (MIP) solvers largely relies on black-box optimization. Each trial requires an expensive solver run and provides only a scalar outcome, so tuning can require many such evaluations. Human experts take a different approach. They inspect solver logs, identify performance bottlenecks, and adjust the parameters that address them. We propose Log-Driven Semantic Tuning (LDST), which uses a large language model (LLM) to automate this process. LDST extracts compact diagnostics from solver logs, uses the LLM to propose sparse edits to the current best configuration based on parameter meanings and observed solver behavior, and validates each proposal before execution. A regime-adaptive objective selects the tuning signal according to the information available from a time-limited run, while a log-based completion signal estimates completion time from branch-and-bound tree growth recorded in ordinary solver logs, so that solved and unsolved runs share one time scale. On 215 instances from five benchmark sets, LDST reduces geometric-mean loss by 43.9% on easy instances and 16.7% on intermediate instances relative to the best of SMAC3, RBFOpt, and random search. In both regimes, LDST achieves a lower loss with 10 proposals than any of these baselines achieves with 50. Configurations that LDST tunes on a single instance also transfer better than baseline configurations to unseen instances of the same family.

items.title: Compressed Oracle Duality: A simple framework for knowing what quantum adversaries know
items.summary: Given a quantum adversary that queries a random oracle, how do we characterize the information that they "know"? The Compressed Oracle method of Zhandry (CRYPTO 2019) is one method that records the queries that the adversary makes; this recording serves as a representation of the information that is learned. However, a significant limitation of the Compressed Oracle method is that it may continue to store information that the adversary has "forgotten." This issue is especially pertinent in the space-bounded setting, where the adversary may uncompute information to free up space, while the information may still reside in the compressed oracle. In this work, we present a simple and interpretable framework called "Compressed Oracle Duality," which extends the Compressed Oracle method for space-bounded algorithms. By applying an isometry to the memory of a quantum adversary, we obtain a pair of compressed oracles with identical marginal distributions and classical correlations which correspond to the knowledge the adversary retains. In fact, we show that the outcome of measuring the new compressed oracle database corresponds exactly to applying the pretty-good measurement on the adversary's memory. As an application of our framework for collision search, we give a simplified proof of the recent $T^2S = Ω(N\log N)$ quantum time-space tradeoff for label-symmetric algorithms due to Magniez-Zur (arXiv:2609.10808); we also prove a stronger classical tradeoff of $TS=Ω(N\log N)$ assuming label symmetry. The proofs under our framework do not require representation theory and instead bound the mutual information between the compressed oracle pairs. This highlights both how the label symmetry assumption bypasses known proof barriers as well as the challenges that remain in achieving unconditional quantum time-space tradeoffs.

items.title: Facility Location with Customer Incompatibilities
items.summary: We study metric facility location with customer incompatibilities, where the clients assigned to each facility must satisfy prescribed independence constraints. We first consider the setting of facility-opening costs and where there is a single matroid $\mathcal M$ over the clients and the set of clients assigned to an open facility must be an independent set in $\mathcal M$. We develop a polynomial-time \((1+\sqrt{2}+ε)\)-approximation algorithm for this setting. We further obtain a polynomial-time \((15+ε)\)-approximation algorithm for the case of non-uniform facility-opening costs when $\mathcal M$ is a partition matroid that only permits $b_g$ clients to be assigned to a facility for each group $g$ in the partition. Both settings are substantial generalizations of Capacitated Facility Location with uniform capacities. Our algorithms are based on local search using add, delete, and single-swap operations. As with CFL, bounding the connection cost is reasonably straightforward using supermodularity of the minimum connection-cost function. However, bounding the facility opening costs requires novel arguments in both cases. We use a ``compression'' argument based on matroid exchange principles to identify a subset of the locally opened facilities whose size is no larger than that of an optimal facility set. The opening costs of facilities outside this subset can be bounded using supermodularity, while bounding the costs of the remaining facilities requires different arguments. It is natural to consider a variant where each possible facility $i$ has its own matroid $\mathcal M_i$ defining the subsets of clients it can feasibly serve. We also show problem is at least as hard to approximate as Set Cover even if all $\mathcal M_i$ are partition matroids that have the same partition of clients, just different group bounds $b_g$.

items.title: Conic Certification of Transformer Attention
items.summary: Attention is the computational core of large language models, yet the verifiers that bound how far an attention head's output can move under input perturbations give no guarantee on how loose their bounds are. A weak certificate therefore cannot be told apart from a fragile model. We develop a conic programming theory of attention certification that supplies this guarantee. We prove that the difficulty lies not in the softmax but in the bilinear interaction of a varying query with the keys. This interaction makes certification NP-hard over boxes and inapproximable once the attention logits can move by a constant amount. A fixed query or listed token substitutions, by contrast, make the exact worst case efficiently computable. An exponential cone moment relaxation then certifies a head with an error bounded quadratically in the perturbation radius by computable quantities, an order that cannot be improved. We also show that relaxations that treat a network one operation at a time, linear bound propagation among them, pay on second-order terms a sum of per-operation maxima instead of one coupled maximum. Computational results on GPT-2 indicate that the theory carries over to a trained model. Against exact worst cases with the query fixed, the certificate attains the predicted second-order accuracy. It is tighter than linear bound propagation on every head, and the looseness of bound propagation tracks the predicted per-operation excess.

items.title: Non-asymptotic analysis of SGLD with discontinuous stochastic gradients: a new route to portfolio CVaR minimization
items.summary: Conditional-Value-at-Risk (CVaR) optimization is a fundamental tool in portfolio selection, yet its nonsmooth loss structure poses a challenge for the existing theory of stochastic gradient methods including associated Langevin algorithms. In particular, the positive-part loss and the softmax portfolio parametrization lead to stochastic gradients that need not be globally Lipschitz continuous, but rather discontinuous, where available non-convex stochastic gradient Langevin dynamics (SGLD) guarantees often exhibit an unfavorable exponential dependence on the problem dimension. In this article, we develop a non-asymptotic analysis of SGLD for a regularized CVaR portfolio optimization problem. We exploit the geometric structure of the CVaR objective to establish linear growth, convexity-at-infinity, and one-sided Lipschitz properties of the stochastic gradient without imposing density assumptions on the asset losses that are typical in previous works. Crucially, the constants appearing in the aforementioned structural conditions are shown to be independent of the number of assets. Moreover, we establish a convergence bound in Wasserstein-2 distance with rate $\mathcal{O}(λ^{1/4})$ and a finite-time guarantee for the expected excess risk. Our analysis, together with the dimension-independent constants in the structural conditions, leads to an excess risk bound that depends linearly on the number of assets. Numerical experiments with simulated Gaussian portfolios exhibit the predicted dimension dependence. Computational comparisons with alternative stochastic optimization methods further illustrate the practical efficiency of SGLD for the optimization problem under consideration. Finally, we extend the framework to a broader class of non-convex stochastic optimization problems with discontinuous stochastic gradients.

items.title: Unconditional optimal convergence of a relaxation Crank-Nicolson difference scheme for 2D space-fractional NLS
items.summary: In this paper, we develop a linearly implicit relaxation Crank-Nicolson difference scheme for the two-dimensional space-fractional nonlinear Schrödinger (SFNS) equation, where the fractional Laplacian is approximated by a simple fractional central difference scheme. The proposed scheme is uniquely solvable and conserves discrete mass for general real-valued nonlinear coefficients, and a modified discrete energy in the cubic case. By introducing a modified error system employing a cut-off technique, we establish the optimal-order error estimates without mesh-ratio restriction. Specifically, the primary variable achieves second-order temporal and spatial convergence in the discrete $H_h^{α/2}$-norm, and the relaxation variable satisfies the same convergence in the discrete $L^2$-norm. Some numerical experiments confirm the relevant theoretical results.

items.title: A Parallel Adaptive Proximal ADMM for Linearly Constrained Separable Composite Optimization Problems
items.summary: We propose and analyze an adaptive proximal alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), based on Jacobi-type updates, for linearly constrained separable nonconvex composite optimization problems. The objective consists of two block-separable functions, one continuously differentiable and weakly convex, and the other convex and Lipschitz continuous. The proposed method is adaptive to all problem parameters and allows inexact solutions of the block proximal subproblems. At each iteration, we solve all block subproblems in parallel, then apply a novel test to decide whether to update the Lagrange multiplier and/or the penalty parameter. Without any rank assumptions on the constraint matrices, we establish an ${\cal O}(ε^{-3})$ iteration-complexity bound for obtaining an approximate first-order stationary point. This matches the best-known complexity for cyclic proximal ADMM methods and improves the existing complexity of Jacobi-type schemes in this general nonconvex setting. Numerical experiments on a nonconvex quadratic program illustrate the proposed method's computational benefits.

items.title: A comparison of parallel iterative methods for ILU triangular solves
items.summary: Exact triangular solves parallelise poorly, limited by the size and number of the level sets, so on GPUs the factors from incomplete LU (ILU) factorisations are often solved approximately with parallel iterative methods. We compare four such methods: a Jacobi method, an Incomplete Sparse Approximate Inverse (ISAI), GMRES polynomials, and AIRG, a reduction multigrid built on GMRES polynomials, for which we introduce a parallel coarse/fine splitting that bounds the diagonal dominance ratio of the fine-fine block. We test them with ILU(0) and ILU(1) factors of canonical PDE problems and 91 SuiteSparse/Matrix Market matrices, the latter on a single GPU. AIRG is the most robust on the PDE factors, with nearly flat iteration counts under refinement and no per-problem tuning, but has the largest setup and memory costs. GMRES polynomials are more robust than the Jacobi method at a similar cost. As the inner solve of an ILU preconditioner with tuned inner iteration counts, ISAI gives the largest median speedups over a hipSPARSE exact triangular solve (4.5$\times$ and 6.8$\times$ for ILU(0) and ILU(1)), though this was dominated by smaller problems; on the largest ILU(1) problems all four methods give similar median speedups of 2.1-2.6$\times$.

items.title: Limits and Constants of OpenAI's Claimed ETH Refutation
items.summary: A recent OpenAI preprint claims a deterministic algorithm that counts the satisfying assignments of a $k$-CNF formula in time $2^{O_k(n\log\log n/\sqrt{\log n})}$, and $2^{O(n/\sqrt{\log n})}$ at bounded clause density, which would refute the Exponential Time Hypothesis. The headline bound is proved by tensor contraction; the body develops an interpolation algorithm with the weaker exponent $n(\log\log n)^2/\sqrt{\log n}$. This note does four things. First, it explains the interpolation algorithm in plain terms. Second, it asks how large $n$ must be for the bounds to bite. The preprint states no constants, so we treat the hidden constant $C$ as a parameter: the general bound beats the $2^n$ of brute force only beyond $n\approx 10^{32}$ for $C=2$, $10^{126}$ for $C=3$ and $10^{3517}$ for $C=10$. We then extract the constants from the tensor-contraction proof: for every input with $m$ clauses at bounded density, the running time it certifies stays above $2^n$ unless $\log_2(n+m)>10^9$, and on random 3-CNF at the satisfiability threshold unless $\log_2 n>5\times10^{11}$. So the bounds are subexponential as $n\to\infty$, but the proof certifies no speed-up over brute force for any input of bounded density that could ever be written down. Third, for the clause-product form of the interpolation algorithm we prove limits in a cost model matching the preprint's evaluation. By a short algebraic lemma, polynomial cost needs components of $O(\log^3 n)$ variables with per-point evaluation, or primal treewidth $O(\log^2 n)$ with dynamic programming over the groups. So the scheme costs $2^{Ω(\sqrt{\mathrm{tw}})}$ at treewidth $\mathrm{tw}$, $2^{Ω(\sqrt n)}$ with high probability on random 3-CNF above clause density 3, and $2^{Ω(n^{1/3})}$ even on trivially countable path formulas. We explain why the preprint's sharper routes escape these limits. Fourth, we report experiments.

items.title: A Hierarchical direct solver for Lippmann-Schwinger equations based on boundary traces
items.summary: A high-order hierarchical direct solver for variable-media scattering in two dimensions is presented. Standard discretizations for these problems produce dense linear systems that are commonly solved iteratively, requiring a new global solve for each incident field. The method proposed here instead constructs a reusable scattering operator for the inhomogeneous medium, based on a hierarchical subdivision of the computational domain. First, high-accuracy leaf scattering operators are built from discretized local integral equations. Up the hierarchy, neighboring boxes are merged to build the scattering operators for successively larger boxes. A key feature of the method is that each scattering operator is represented as a map of incoming traces to outgoing traces. Consequently, volume unknowns appear only in the leaf computations; all higher levels of the hierarchy operate entirely on boundary traces. The hierarchical solver is presented first at the continuum level and discretized only afterward using high-order local volume quadrature, polynomial trace representations, and boundary integral techniques. For a discretization involving $N$ degrees of freedom, the method requires $O(N^{3/2})$ work and $O(N\log N)$ storage to build all scattering operators. Once these are available, any incoming field can be processed at cost $O(N)$ if only the outgoing field is required, and cost $O(N\log N)$ if the full field is required. Numerical experiments demonstrate high-order accuracy on a range of challenging scattering problems including cavities, back-scattering, limited regularity, and high wavenumber, that pose significant challenges to iterative methods.

items.title: $k$-Center under Weak and Strong Distance Oracles with an Application to Minimum Sum of Radii Clustering
items.summary: In the weak-strong distance oracle model of Bateni, Dharangutte, Jayaram and Wang (COLT 2024), a metric $(X,d)$ on $n$ points is accessed through two oracles: a cheap weak oracle that returns each queried distance correctly with probability $1-δ$ and permits arbitrary values on corrupted pairs, chosen by an adversary who knows the entire metric and all corrupted pairs, and an expensive strong oracle that reveals a point exactly. The goal is to cluster well while making as few strong queries as possible. Our main result is a $(6+\varepsilon)$-approximation for $k$-center using $O(k\log n\log(\varepsilon^{-1}\log n))$ strong point queries, for any fixed $\varepsilon>0$. This improves both the $(14+\varepsilon)$ approximation factor and the $O(k\log^2 n\log(\varepsilon^{-1}\log n))$ query bound of Bateni et al. It also improves the query complexity of the recent $(6+\varepsilon)$-approximation of Pradhan, Bhattacharya and Jaiswal (AISTATS 2026), in the variant of the model they study. Our algorithm outputs an explicitly known sketch of an otherwise unknown metric: a concrete metric on at most $k$ points that a downstream algorithm can compute with directly, with no further queries and no noise. As an application, we give a simple FPT algorithm for Minimum Sum of Radii (MSR) that returns a constant-factor solution using $2^{O(k\log k)}\cdot O(\log n\log\log n)$ strong queries. We complement the upper bound with an $Ω(k\log(n/k))$ lower bound for $k$-center with assignment that holds for row-local algorithms. These algorithms assign two unqueried points to the same center whenever their weak distances to the strong-queried points are exactly the same. Our algorithm and those of Bateni et al. and Pradhan et al. are all row-local, so our query bound is optimal for this class up to the $O(\log\log n)$ factor.

items.title: Learning to evolve by matching velocities
items.summary: Learning the continuous-time evolution of nonlinear dynamical systems relies on trajectory-based objectives, which require simulating the learned dynamics during training and backpropagating through the numerical scheme, at a cost that grows with the rollout horizon. We show that trajectory-based objectives degenerate as the rollout horizon increases, hindering gradient-based optimization, and that the numerical scheme biases the learned dynamics by constraining the spectrum of the learned Jacobian to its absolute stability region. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Velocity Matching (VM), a simulation-free objective that relies on piecewise-linear interpolation and stochastic collocation, and approximates the velocity population risk to second order in the sampling step. We develop a theoretical framework for velocity-based learning, introducing stability estimates that control trajectory errors in terms of velocity errors, which enable us to establish universal and continuous-time approximation results when the learned velocity field is parameterized by deep neural networks. Building on a bias-variance decomposition of the VM objective, we show that its higher-order approximation of the velocity population risk yields a consistent minimizer; that it relates to the residual of an A-stable continuous-stage Runge-Kutta scheme, thus connecting VM to implicit integration without requiring any implicit solve; and that it implicitly matches the action of the learned Jacobian to that of the true one along the observed trajectories, without requiring access to the underlying velocity field or its Jacobian. Numerical experiments on nonlinear ordinary differential equations and semi-discretized time-dependent partial differential equations show that VM improves accuracy over trajectory-based objectives, while avoiding both the cost of simulation and the instabilities of long rollouts.

items.title: Max Weight Independent Set in graphs with no long claws nor large induced bicliques
items.summary: The complexity of Max Weight Independent Set (MWIS) in graphs excluding a fixed subdivided claw is one of the central open problems in algorithmic graph theory. We show that MWIS can be solved in polynomial time in graphs excluding a fixed subdivided claw and a fixed biclique as an induced subgraph. This strengthens a result of Abrishami, Chudnovsky, Dibek, Pilipczuk, and Rzążewski [ACM TALG 2026] who showed an analogous result, but under a stronger assumption that some biclique is excluded as a subgraph.

items.title: Online carpooling against an oblivious adversary
items.summary: In the online carpooling problem, edges on $n$ vertices arrive one at a time and must be oriented immediately, so as to keep the difference between the indegree and the outdegree of every vertex small. We give a randomized online algorithm which bounds the largest absolute difference over the first $T$ edges by $O((\log T)^{1/3})$ with high probability on every input sequence fixed in advance. This proves a conjecture of Kulkarni, Reis and Rothvoss and matches the known worst case lower bound. The algorithm keeps the law of the discrepancy vector dominated in the convex order by a Gaussian measure, and forces the endpoint with the smaller discrepancy to receive the edge whenever the two discrepancies are far apart. In the analysis we show that a vertex of discrepancy $D$ is preceded by a set of $O(D)$ vertices with total discrepancy $Ω(D^2)$.

items.title: Hamiltonian Cycle Construction in Rectangular Grid Graphs with Three-Stacked Triangular Holes
items.summary: The Hamiltonian cycle problem is NP-complete for general grid graphs, while several structured classes admit efficient construction algorithms. In this paper, we investigate Hamiltonian cycle construction in rectangular grid graphs containing a three-stacked right-triangular hole. We explore two complementary approaches based on the geometric structure of the hole and the parity properties of rectangular subgraphs. The first approach constructs a Hamiltonian path in the complementary reversed staircase region, extends it into an inner Hamiltonian cycle, and merges it with a cycle in the surrounding graph. The second approach partitions the graph into six rectangular subgraphs and constructs a global Hamiltonian cycle by merging local cycles along compatible boundaries. When odd-sized rectangular subgraphs prevent direct cycle construction, we develop parity-based repartitioning techniques that transform selected configurations into even-sized rectangles. We provide constructions for adjacent and nonadjacent odd-sized configurations and investigate reductions for cases involving multiple odd-sized regions. These results establish a constructive framework for Hamiltonian cycles in grid graphs with staircase-shaped holes and identify the remaining cases requiring further analysis.

items.title: Optimistic Gradient Algorithms with Randomized Coordinate and Variance Reduction Strategies for Composite Inclusions
items.summary: In this paper, we consider a class of possibly nonmonotone finite-sum composite inclusions in which evaluating all components or updating all coordinates at every iteration can be computationally expensive. We develop two optimistic gradient frameworks that combine variance reduction with randomized block-coordinate updates. The first framework applies under a blockwise average Lipschitz continuity condition and the existence of a weak-Minty solution. It achieves an $\mathcal{O}(1/k)$ convergence rate for the expected squared residual, and its iterates converge almost surely under mild additional conditions. The second framework relies on a backward-forward reformulation under average co-coercivity and co-hypomonotonicity. It achieves faster $\mathcal{O}(1/k^2)$ and $o(1/k^2)$ rates for the expected squared residual, as well as $o(1/k^2)$ almost-sure rates. For both frameworks, we provide a generic condition on the stochastic estimator that covers mini-batch, loopless SVRG, and a generalized JacSketch-type estimator, and we derive the corresponding oracle complexities under importance-based block sampling. In particular, in highly heterogeneous regimes, the L-SVRG and JacSketch variants attain $\mathcal{O}\big(n + n^{2/3}ε^{-2}\big)$ and $\mathcal{O}\big(n + n^{2/3}ε^{-1}\big)$ oracle complexities for the nonaccelerated and accelerated methods, respectively. Numerical experiments illustrate the effects of variance reduction and block-coordinate sampling, and compare the proposed methods with existing baselines.

items.title: Catenary Visibility: A Geometric Framework for Planning with Tethered Robots
items.summary: This paper introduces \emph{catenary visibility}, a new geometric visibility concept for a robotic system consisting of a ground robot tethered to an aerial drone. The tether is modeled as an extensible catenary curve with bounded length, providing sustained power and significantly extending operational range. We define a point on the ground plane as \emph{catenary-visible} from a target point in 3D if there exists a collision-free catenary connecting them, given a set of obstacles. This paper introduces a geometric framework for visibility-aware planning of a tethered marsupial system, addressing the computational challenge of determining the feasible deployment locus: the collection of points in the ground plane that are catenary-visible from a given target in 3D space. We begin by solving the 2D subproblem, where the obstacles, target, and the ground vehicle's line of motion are all constrained to a single vertical plane. Our algorithm for this case computes the complete set of feasible launch points along the motion line and simultaneously determines the range of viable cable lengths for each. We also consider the query problem of finding all collision-free length ranges for a given location of the ground robot. Building upon this planar solution, we then generalize the approach to three dimensions, deriving a 3D solution for a constrained class of obstacles.

items.title: Variance-reduced First-order Methods for Finite-sum Function Constrained Convex Optimization
items.summary: This paper studies finite-sum convex optimization with convex function constraints, where both the objective $f(x)=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(x)$ and the constraint mapping $g(x)=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{j=1}^n g_j(x)$ may have a large number of components. We propose a variance-reduced anchored constraint extrapolation method (VaRAn-ConEx), which combines stochastic component sampling with primal--dual extrapolation for nonlinear function constraints. Relative to stochastic approximation schemes such as ConEx, VaRAn-ConEx~method reduces gradient complexity by using epoch-wise full-gradient correction and variance-reduced estimators for both the objective and constraint components. In the semi-finite case where $n=1$, the method attains gradient complexities $O(\sqrt m/ε)$ under constant steps and $O(m/ε^{1/2}+1/ε^{3/2})$ under nonconstant steps. In the fully finite-sum case, we establish boundedness of the Lagrange multiplier sequence and derive convergence and gradient-complexity bounds for constant and nonconstant step-size policies. Under these policies, we then prove similar gradient complexity with $m$ replaced by $\max\{m,n\}$. We also show acceleration when the finite-sum objective $f$ is strongly convex, irrespective of components $f_i$.

items.title: Costate Estimation and Covector Mapping for Bernstein Polynomial Direct Methods in Optimal Control
items.summary: Bernstein polynomial approximation of continuous functions has a slower rate of convergence as compared to other approximation methods. ``The fact seems to have precluded any numerical application of Bernstein polynomials from having been made. Perhaps they will find application when the properties of the approximant in the large are of more importance than the closeness of the approximation.'' -- has remarked P.J. Davis in his 1963 book Interpolation and Approximation. This paper presents a direct approximation method for nonlinear optimal control problems with mixed input and state constraints based on Bernstein polynomial approximation, in which the dynamic and path constraints are imposed at the Bernstein coefficients (control points). We provide a rigorous analysis showing that, under convergence assumptions on the control polygons, the proposed method yields consistent approximations of time continuous optimal control problems and can be used for costate estimation of the optimal control problems. In particular, multipliers satisfying a relaxed Karush Kuhn Tucker system of the resulting nonlinear program, scaled by the quadrature weight, approximate the costate and the multipliers of the optimal control problem. Owing to the structure of the Bernstein differentiation matrix, the discrete transversality conditions are contained in the relaxed Karush Kuhn Tucker system, and no additional closure conditions need to be added to it. This result leads to the formulation of the Covector Mapping Theorem for Bernstein polynomial approximation.

items.title: A Preconditioned Semismooth Newton Method for Box-Constrained Elliptic Optimal Control Problems with Random Coefficients
items.summary: We consider the optimal control problem of an elliptic PDE with random diffusion under pointwise box constraints on the control. The constraints make the optimality conditions nonsmooth, with an active set that is not known in advance, and the random diffusion couples the state and the adjoint across all stochastic modes. To design a solution algorithm for this problem, we rely on the Fenchel duality viewpoint. Fenchel duality absorbs the box constraint into the objective and yields an exact reduced problem in the elliptic adjoint variable alone. After a stochastic Galerkin--finite element discretization, eliminating the state leaves a strongly monotone, piecewise smooth equation, which we solve directly by a matrix-free semismooth Newton method with the box projection retained exactly and with no outer iteration, penalty or smoothing parameter. Next, we introduce and analyze a current-set preconditioner, which adds the active-set correction of the current Newton step to a mean-diffusion reference operator and is inverted exactly by a rank-1 update. For implementation, we use a cheaper preconditioner that keeps only a fraction of free control values. Numerical experiments show second-order convergence of the state, and Newton and PCG counts that stay bounded under mesh refinement and growth of the stochastic dimension.

items.title: Constant Approximation of Fréchet Distance in Near-Linear Time
items.summary: We present a deterministic algorithm that approximates the Fréchet distance between two polygonal curves in $\mathbb{R}^d$ with $n$ and $m$ vertices within a constant factor in $O((m+n)^{1+\varepsilon})$ time, for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$ and fixed dimension $d$. The approximation factor depends only on $\varepsilon$ and $d$. No assumption on the input curves is needed, and the algorithm also reports a matching certifying the approximation. The same result holds for the discrete Fréchet distance. Our result extends the line of work initiated by Cheng, Huang, and Zhang (2025), who gave the first constant-factor approximation in strongly subquadratic time, to near-linear time. For two $n$-vertex curves, the best previous running time was $\widetilde{O}(n^{5/3})$, due to van der Horst and Ophelders (2026). Our algorithm bootstraps between two primitives: a data structure that preprocesses a single curve for comparing any two of its subcurves, and a query procedure that compares subcurves of two different curves. Given the data structure for one curve, we compare it with another curve using a surrogate assembled from subcurves of the former. The surrogate is shared by all possible starting points of a matching. Conversely, faster queries make the next data structure cheaper to build. After a number of rounds that depends only on $\varepsilon$, both preprocessing and query time are $O((m+n)^{1+\varepsilon})$. To make each round's output reusable by the next, we compactly summarize how matchings can enter and leave a pair of subcurves. These summaries can be applied to different starting points and retain the information needed to report the matchings.

items.title: ProLand: A New Infeasible Manifold Optimization Method for LoRA Fine-Tuning
items.summary: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) enables parameter-efficient fine-tuning but can suffer from redundant basis directions. Constraining the basis factor to the Stiefel manifold addresses this redundancy through orthonormality. Landing methods allow temporarily infeasible iterates to explore a neighborhood of the manifold while progressively restoring orthogonality without per-step retractions. To improve optimization efficiency while retaining this flexibility, we introduce ProLand (Product-space Landing), a retraction-free optimizer that combines coordinated factor updates with Muon-style spectral directions. By designing the updates in the space of the represented weight increment, ProLand separates objective optimization from orthogonality restoration, supporting efficient feasibility recovery. This coordinated construction also enables Muon-style directions to guide objective optimization while preserving that separation. Experiments cover four GLUE validation tasks on DeBERTa-v3-base and seven language benchmarks on Qwen2.5-3B, Llama-3.2-3B, and Moonlight-16B-A3B across multiple adapter ranks. Across these 11 tasks, ProLand achieves the highest average score among the compared methods in every tested encoder and decoder model-rank configuration.

items.title: Parameter-Free First-Order Method for Constrained Variational Inequalities
items.summary: Constrained variational inequalities (VIs) provide a general framework for modeling and solving complementarity and equilibrium problems with functional constraints. In this paper, we propose a parameter-free accelerated operator sliding (PFAOS) method for solving monotone VIs with convex smooth constraints. For a single constraint, PFAOS achieves an operator evaluation complexity of $\mathcal{O}(1/\varepsilon)$ and a constraint gradient evaluation complexity of $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{\varepsilon})$, without requiring prior knowledge of the Lipschitz constant of the VI operator or the smoothness constant of the constraint function. We further extend PFAOS to multiple constraints by incorporating a primal-dual hybrid gradient update, yielding a multi-constrained PFAOS (MC-PFAOS) method that preserves the same evaluation complexities. Finally, numerical experiments are conducted on large-scale games with coupling constraints to validate the efficiency and effectiveness of the proposed algorithms.

items.title: Wave Forcing: Towards Speed-of-Light Streaming Video Generation
items.summary: Real-time long-video generation requires continuous output with consistent appearance and natural motion. Existing chunk-wise autoregressive methods face challenges in both generation efficiency and long-video quality: serialized denoising and history-cache refresh require two forward passes even with one-step denoising, and longer rollouts can degrade quality and cause camera drift. We propose Wave Forcing (WF), which co-designs generation, training, and execution for continuous video output with multi-step denoising. WF uses chunk-wise causal attention to access earlier, cleaner chunks before their denoising is complete, and distributes staggered denoising and cache-refresh stages across full-model replicas to achieve 1F1C: one output chunk per concurrent forward round after pipeline fill. To adapt the model to this continuous generation process, we develop a three-stage training procedure that successively introduces mixed-noise denoising, motion supervision, and causal adaptation using self-generated history. To execute this process efficiently, Wave Runtime (WaveRT) uses Wave Parallelism (WP) for early K/V delivery and communication-computation overlap, together with optimized kernels and pipelined VAE decoding. Experiments on Wan2.1-T2V-1.3B show that 5-step WF maintains overall quality comparable to Rolling Forcing while achieving higher Dynamic Degree on both short and long videos. Our system efficiency experiments show that 4-step WF achieves 147.6 DiT FPS and 134.8 end-to-end FPS on eight H200 GPUs, yielding 7.07x the single-GPU end-to-end throughput. In DiT-only tests with matched SageAttention+W8A8 backends, denoising steps, and GPU counts, WP delivers up to 2.53x the throughput of the faster of the Ulysses and Ring context-parallel baselines across six model scales (1.3B-14B).

items.title: Video Generation Meets Agent Harness: Agentic Video Generation, Agentic World Modeling and Recursive Self-Improvement
items.summary: Video generation is shifting from end-to-end synthesis toward agentic generation, where planning, tool use, and feedback enable coherent, controllable multi-shot videos. In parallel, video world models provide action-conditioned observations and predicted futures, serving as interactive environments for agents. We study their intersection through the agent harness: an executable runtime that constructs context, exposes tools, maintains state, routes feedback, and manages budgets around video models. This report examines three directions. First, agentic video generation, where harnesses coordinate scripting, shot planning, asset management, production, and editing, alongside the evaluation challenges of these systems. Second, agentic world modeling, where harnesses mediate observation, control, execution, and state. We discuss hybrid designs in which game engines or agent-written programs maintain world state while video models render observations, and how agents and world models can mutually evaluate and improve one another. Third, recursive self-improvement (RSI) in video model development, distinguishing output revisions, updates to harness state, generator parameters, and evaluators, and changes to the improvement procedure itself. We identify how these improvements feed back into subsequent development. Across these directions, we analyze essential agent capabilities, including audiovisual perception, long-horizon planning, memory, code-based interaction, feedback-guided control, skill reuse, and multi-agent coordination. We conclude with challenges in autonomous video production, lifelong memory, programmable hybrid control, autonomous model development, provenance, cost accounting, and evaluation linking video quality and task performance to sustained improvements in models and harnesses.

items.title: Democratizing Robot-Use Agents: A Unified Harness with Open Models
items.summary: Robot-use Agents (RUAs) have shown promising zero-shot manipulation capabilities, but reliance on frontier, proprietary models limits research into further training. To democratize RUA research, we introduce uni-robot-agent, a unified harness for competitive open-weight robot use that supports further training. Without privileged inputs, an out-of-the-box Qwen3.8-Flash-Next achieves a RoboDojo Score of 31.39, surpassing the published GPT-6 Astra-RoboProbe result of 28.97 and many VLA/WAM baselines, and performs competitively on 19 real-world tasks. Our analysis across model generations, families, and sizes links effective robot use to four general capabilities, suggesting that future RUA training should develop them jointly.

items.title: From Fragmentation to Fusion: A Survey and Roadmap for Omnimodal Embeddings
items.summary: Embedding models underpin virtually every modern AI system, from search engines to recommendation systems. Despite shared mathematical foundations, research on embedding models remains fragmented by modality: the communities develop largely in isolation, seldom exchanging insights. We argue that this fragmentation obscures a deeper convergence. Driven by contrastive learning, Transformer architectures, and a granularity shift, embedding research across modalities is converging toward a common set of principles, even as modality-specific challenges remain underexplored. To reason across this convergence without conflating it, we propose a framework of three progressively harder capabilities: coverage, comparability, and compositionality. Three paths toward unification satisfy these in turn: transformation broadens coverage, alignment enables comparability, and joint embedding, the terminus we advocate, aims at compositionality. This position paper traces the resulting evolution, providing the first unified, cross-cutting treatment of omnimodal embedding research.

items.title: NorthCUA Technical Report: Turbocharging Computer-Use Agents through Experience at Scale
items.summary: Scaling computer-use agents from individual actions to complex software work requires experience that connects decisions to complete outcomes. We present NorthCUA, an integrated system for turbocharging computer-use agents through experience at scale. Its Experience Flywheel supplies diverse executable tasks to the NorthCUA Harness, which sustains long interactions, records decisions, and checks task outcomes. The Flywheel uses these records to curate verified trajectories. For unsolved tasks, recursive self-improvement evolves reusable skills and preserves verified milestones so later attempts build on earlier progress. Staged Learning combines this experience with grounding data from the Flywheel to develop GUI competence through mid-training and long-horizon supervised fine-tuning. The policy then learns from fresh attempts in the same Harness through joint desktop-web reinforcement learning, closing the loop between experience production and policy improvement. The resulting Nano, Mini, and Pro family achieves state-of-the-art results among open-source models across GUI grounding, desktop execution, and Web interaction under the reported evaluation settings. For more responsive Web workflows, NorthCUA-Ultrafast pairs direct action selection with open-ended generation on pre-RL Nano, offering a measured quality-latency tradeoff. Together, these advances establish NorthCUA as a high-performing model family and a reusable foundation for agents that carry complex software work from intent to completion.

items.title: Diagnosing the Reference Gap: What Visual Scaffolds Can and Cannot Fix in Multimodal Reasoning
items.summary: Multimodal large language models can recognize visual content yet struggle to reason reliably over it across multiple steps. In counting, a model may see all objects but lose track of which ones it has counted. We argue that such failures, commonly attributed to perception, reveal a reference gap: the failure to bind language to the relevant visual entities, regions, or locations. Motivated by the theory of visual routines, we test whether external references such as numbering can narrow this gap. We introduce ReGap-Bench, a paired benchmark of five visual reasoning tasks in which the scene, question, and answer are fixed and only the reference varies. Results show that task-matched references improve accuracy by up to 25\%, while mismatched references provide little benefit or even hurt performance. These findings identify the reference gap as a bottleneck distinct from visual perception and show that constructing task-appropriate visual references can serve as a training-free visual skill for improving multimodal reasoning.

items.title: DeFT-RAG: Decomposing Multi-Hop Questions into Self-Contained Sub-Questions with Reusable Answers
items.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) lets a large language model (LLM) answer questions by retrieving relevant passages from a large corpus. However, RAG struggles with multi-hop questions, which require chaining facts spread across several documents through intermediate entities that the question never mentions. Graph-based RAG methods retrieve once from the entities a question names and so rarely recover the full evidence chain. Iterative RAG methods recover it step by step, but their accuracy is limited by the many tasks they ask the LLM to perform, such as planning the sub-questions, deciding their dependencies, rewriting them as answers arrive, and keeping track of what is known. We propose DeFT-RAG, a RAG framework built on three components. First, DeFT-RAG generates one self-contained sub-question at a time from the original question and the sub-questions answered so far with their answers (QA pairs). Each sub-question names every entity it asks about, which removes the need to plan, track dependencies or rewrite, and lets the LLM focus on a single fine-grained task at a time. Second, DeFT-RAG moves the remaining LLM work outside the LLM: rule-based updates to a QA table that keeps track of what is known, and yes/no decisions made by a fine-tuned lightweight decision model. Third, DeFT-RAG caches the QA pairs and reuses an answer when a later question asks a sub-question with the same meaning. On MuSiQue, 2WikiMultiHopQA and HotpotQA, DeFT-RAG achieves the best accuracy among thirteen baselines with both gpt-4o-mini and Qwen3.6 as the backbone, while giving the LLM fewer input tokens than any other iterative method. With a QA cache shared across 1,000 MuSiQue questions, 23.1% of sub-questions are answered from the cache, which reduces LLM calls by 12.9% without lowering accuracy.

items.title: Lost in Recovery: Demystifying Recovery Behavior of Computer-Use Agents via Goal-Oriented Action Replay
items.summary: Recent advances in large (vision) language models have enabled computer-use agents that automate digital workflows via fine-grained keyboard and mouse operations. However, such agents remain fragile in long-horizon settings, where errors accumulate and executed actions leave unintended side effects, making the ability to recover from failures critical. Yet, existing remedies remain inadequate: environment resets are infeasible in proprietary settings, action replay is prohibitively expensive over long horizons, and API-based rollback is limited to web environments, leaving model-based recovery largely unexplored. To address this gap, we present ReTrace, a scalable evaluation framework for systematically studying recovery behavior in computer-use agents. We formalize Transition-Consistent Recovery: identical downstream actions from the recovered and target states must yield identical outcomes. We operationalize this criterion through goal-oriented action replay following controlled error injection. Using ReTrace, we present the first systematic study of autonomous, model-based recovery, revealing that (i) ideal recovery can unlock model's latent task completion capabilities, (ii) current computer-use agents fail to exploit their latent recovery capabilities, and (iii) accurate model-based recovery yields measurable end-to-end gains. Together, these findings establish recovery as a fundamental capability for building reliable computer-use agents. Our code and dataset is available at https://github.com/BangProx/ReTRACE.

items.title: MAServeBench: Benchmarking Multi-Agent LLM Serving Systems with Hierarchical Collaboration Workloads
items.summary: Large language model (LLM)-based multi-agent systems (MAS) coordinate specialized agents to solve complex tasks, turning each user request into interdependent model and tool operations. Unlike independent requests, these operations become ready at different times and consume evolving context as agents coordinate and exchange results. This creates changing patterns of concurrency, computation, and memory demand that can expose different bottlenecks in LLM serving hardware. Yet benchmarking these effects requires capturing the collaboration rules that generate serving workloads, beyond the requests observed during execution. We present MAServeBench, a benchmark that treats multi-agent collaboration as a configurable dimension of serving workloads for LLM serving and hardware evaluation. Its composable stages capture how agents coordinate and exchange context in documented MAS workflows, enabling native executions to generate different workloads even when task inputs and tools remain unchanged.
